what: 1. Load raw data from a directory
title: Getting started with classydms
text: expected file layout one file per subject, disease control samples separate folders. file tab-delimited GC-DMS layout described ?read_dms_file (line 1 = “Vc”, line 2 = tab + CV values, line 3 = header, lines 4+ = time + intensities). Channel choice: classifiers package train positive ion channel (POS files). Negative-channel data used. default pattern enforces — pass explicit pattern argument need different channel filename convention. non-standard file format, write loader produces list shape — element must $path, $time, $cv, $Z, outer list meaningful (non-empty) names. long contract met, rest pipeline works unchanged.
code: # One-shot loader: reads all files matching the POS-channel pattern, # skips broken ones, names each sample after its file basename (so # results stay traceable to subjects), and returns a (samples, y) pair. disease_dir = here::here("sampledata/influenza") control_dir = here::here("sampledata/controls")  loaded <- load_dms_directory(   disease_dir = disease_dir,   control_dir = control_dir,   pattern     = "POS.*\\.(xls|txt|tsv|csv)$"  # POS channel only — see note )  samples <- loaded$samples   # named list, each element has $path, $time, $cv, $Z y       <- loaded$y         # named integer vector: 2 = disease, 1 = control  # Sample names map to file basenames without extensions, so you can: samples[["241115-S1994-S1-DMS1_POS"]]    # index by subject names(samples)                            # see the full list of subjects  # Sanity check stopifnot(is.list(samples), length(samples) > 0,           is.matrix(samples[[1]]$Z),           all(nzchar(names(samples))))   # no empty-string names

title: Getting started with classydms
code: # Savitzky-Golay smoothing + AsLS baseline correction + clip below zero samples_proc <- lapply(samples, process_one_sample,                         sg_p = 3, sg_n = 21,                         asls_lambda = 1e6, asls_p = 0.01, asls_niter = 10)  # Dust threshold each sample to a fixed floor (e.g. global value, or # per-sample via robust_eps). For a fixed floor: dust_thr <- 0.005 samples_dust <- lapply(samples_proc, baseline_basement,                         basement_thr = dust_thr)  # Cohort-wide trim bounds b_list <- lapply(samples_dust,                   function(s) trim_bounds_from_occupancy(s$Z)) R0 <- max(sapply(samples_dust, function(s) nrow(s$Z))) C0 <- max(sapply(samples_dust, function(s) ncol(s$Z))) global_b <- pooled_trim_bounds(b_list, R = R0, C = C0,                                 q_lo = 0.05, q_hi = 0.95) samples_trimmed <- lapply(samples_dust, trim_sample, bounds = global_b)  # Per-sample log-quantile normalization + pad to common size Z_norm   <- map(samples_trimmed, ~normalize_sample(.x$Z)) pad_dims <- compute_pad_targets(Z_norm) Z_padded <- map(Z_norm, ~pad_to_target(.x, pad_dims$H, pad_dims$W))

what: Why elastic net on encoder features?
title: Interpretability and biomarker localization
text: global average pooling, sample represented 64-dimensional feature vector. ~200 labeled samples, fitting classifier ~130 free parameters (logistic regression 64 features + intercept) well-conditioned. elastic net penalty adds two extras: shrinkage (avoids overconfident weights given limited data) built-feature selection (channels aren’t useful zeroed exactly). interpretable head can put frozen encoder: coefficient channel cc literally tells much unit increase channel’s mean activation pushes predicted log-odds toward disease.

code: coef_df <- tibble(   channel  = seq_len(64),   coef     = elnet$coefs,   abs_coef = abs(elnet$coefs) ) %>%   mutate(direction = case_when(     coef > 0 ~ "higher in disease",     coef < 0 ~ "higher in control",     TRUE     ~ "zero"   ))  n_active <- sum(coef_df$coef != 0) message(n_active, " of 64 channels have non-zero coefficients")  coef_df %>%   filter(coef != 0) %>%   mutate(channel = factor(channel, levels = channel[order(-abs_coef)])) %>%   ggplot(aes(x = channel, y = coef, fill = direction)) +   geom_col() +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("higher in disease" = "steelblue",                                 "higher in control" = "coral")) +   labs(title = "Elastic net coefficients on encoder features",        subtitle = paste0(n_active, " of 64 channels predictive"),        x = "Encoder channel (sorted by importance)", y = "Coefficient") +   theme_minimal()

title: Interpretability and biomarker localization
text: elastic net classifier head linear global-average-pooled features. means can compute per-sample spatial saliency map analytically, without backpropagation: Si(h,w)=∑c=164β̂c⋅Fi(c)(h,w) S_i(h, w) \;=\; \sum_{c=1}^{64} \hat{\beta}_c \cdot F_i^{(c)}(h, w) Fi(c)F_i^{(c)} encoder’s spatial feature map channel cc sample ii, β̂c\hat{\beta}_c elastic net coefficient channel. Bilinearly upsampled input resolution, SiS_i 2-D map positive (red) regions push toward “disease” prediction negative (blue) regions push toward “control.” mathematically equivalent Class Activation Mapping (CAM) elastic net coefficients head weights, similar spirit Grad-CAM without requiring backpropagation.

what: Level 3 — From saliency hotspots to (RT, CV) coordinates
title: Interpretability and biomarker localization
text: aggregated saliency maps live padded image coordinates. name candidate biomarkers, need convert physical retention time (seconds) compensation voltage (volts) original instrument. samples_trimmed objects retain time cv vectors exactly purpose. now list physical (RT, CV) coordinates ranked saliency magnitude. next step — outside scope classydms — cross-reference coordinates co-analyzed standards compound library covering instrument’s RT/CV grid. hotspot becomes candidate biomarker compound.
code: # Use any one sample's time/cv as the reference axes (they're shared # across the cohort after global trimming + center-padding) time_axis <- samples_trimmed[[1]]$time cv_axis   <- samples_trimmed[[1]]$cv H_real    <- length(time_axis) W_real    <- length(cv_axis)  # Crop the saliency to the actual data region (top-left of padded image) sal_diff_real <- sal_diff[seq_len(H_real), seq_len(W_real)]  sal_phys <- expand.grid(rt = time_axis, cv = cv_axis) %>%   mutate(value = as.numeric(sal_diff_real))  # Identify top hotspots (top 1% of |saliency|) threshold <- quantile(abs(sal_phys$value), 0.99) hotspots <- sal_phys %>%   filter(abs(value) >= threshold) %>%   arrange(desc(abs(value))) %>%   slice_head(n = 20)  hotspots

title: Pre-training in depth
text: Clinical GC-DMS cohorts typically contain 100–200 subjects. Training deep convolutional encoder labeled examples leads severe overfitting: network memorizes training set rather learning generalizable features. Transfer learning sidesteps first training encoder large auxiliary dataset (labels needed), resulting weights good starting point actual classification task. classydms synthetic data matched cohort. synthetic generator builds 2-D Gaussian “peaks” locations, widths, intensities sampled distributions estimated empirically real spectra. Pretraining encoder reconstruct denoise synthetic images forces learn morphology GC-DMS data — peaks background, sparse signal large image, characteristic spatial scales — without ever seeing class label. two pretraining entry points: real classification work online variant strongly recommended. rest article focuses .

what: Step 2 — Visualize synthetic vs real samples (sanity check)
title: Pre-training in depth
text: launching long pretraining run, generate synthetic samples compare real ones eye. single important sanity check. want two rows look qualitatively similar : number peaks, range peak sizes, spatial distribution across RT CV, noise level. synthetic samples far fewer peaks, peaks size, peaks bunched one region, revisit peak_params — usually top_k, frac_height, inspecting peak_params$rt_loc_raw distributions.

code: library(classydms)  # 1. Load raw data (samples_keep, y_keep) using your project-specific loader # 2. Preprocess samples_proc <- lapply(samples_keep, process_one_sample) b_list <- lapply(samples_proc, function(s) trim_bounds_from_occupancy(s$Z)) R0 <- max(sapply(samples_proc, function(s) nrow(s$Z))) C0 <- max(sapply(samples_proc, function(s) ncol(s$Z))) global_b <- pooled_trim_bounds(b_list, R = R0, C = C0) samples_trimmed <- lapply(samples_proc, trim_sample, bounds = global_b)  Z_norm   <- purrr::map(samples_trimmed, ~normalize_sample(.x$Z)) pad_dims <- compute_pad_targets(Z_norm) Z_padded <- purrr::map(Z_norm, ~pad_to_target(.x, pad_dims$H, pad_dims$W))  # 3. Estimate peak parameters from real data (label-agnostic) Z_raw     <- purrr::map(samples_trimmed, ~.x$Z) Z_pretrim <- purrr::map(samples_trimmed,                           ~if (!is.null(.x$Z_pretrim)) .x$Z_pretrim else .x$Z) peak_params <- estimate_peak_params(Z_raw, Z_pretrim_list = Z_pretrim,                                      top_k = 150, frac_height = 0.5)  # 4. Self-supervised pretraining (recommended: online, for memory efficiency) pretrain_result <- pretrain_denoising_online(   peak_params,   H = pad_dims$H, W = pad_dims$W,   steps_per_epoch = 1000L, epochs = 50L, batch_size = 32L,   save_path = "encoder.pt" )  # 5. Classify with elastic net on encoder features elnet <- cv_encoder_elastic_net(pretrain_result$encoder,                                  Z_list = Z_padded, y = y_keep,                                  k = 5, alpha = 0.5) elnet$auc elnet$coefs    # which of the 64 channels matter  # 6. Spatial saliency map for biomarker localization disease_idx <- which(y_keep == 2) orig_dims <- lapply(samples_trimmed, function(s) c(H = nrow(s$Z), W = ncol(s$Z))) sal <- aggregate_saliency_masked(pretrain_result$encoder, Z_padded,                                    coefs = elnet$coefs,                                    sample_indices = disease_idx,                                    orig_dims = orig_dims) # sal is a 2-D matrix in padded image coordinates; map back to RT/CV using # samples_trimmed[[1]]$time and samples_trimmed[[1]]$cv
